items.prose: An adventure park strings a straight zip wire between two platforms. The start platform is 14 m above the ground and the end platform is 2 m above it. The platforms stand 35 m apart, measured along the level ground.

parts.question: The wire, the drop between the platforms and the level gap make a right-angled triangle. How long is the wire, in metres? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: The drop is $14 - 2 = 12$ m, so the wire is $\sqrt{12^2 + 35^2} = \sqrt{1369} = 37$ m.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the drop between the platforms first, then use Pythagoras.

byKey.added: You added the two sides. The wire is the hypotenuse: square the sides, add, then take the root.
byKey.used-14: You used 14 m for the drop. The wire falls from 14 m to 2 m, so the drop is $14 - 2 = 12$ m.
byKey.subtracted: You subtracted the squares. The wire faces the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse: add the squares.

explain.text: The drop between the platforms is $14 - 2 = 12$ m. The wire faces the right angle, so $12^2 + 35^2 = 144 + 1225 = 1369$. The wire is $\sqrt{1369} = 37$ m.

parts.question: Let $\theta$ be the angle the wire makes with the level. Using a wire of 37 m and a drop of 12 m, what is $\sin\theta$? Give it as a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Name the sides from the angle at the start: the drop is opposite and the wire is the hypotenuse.

byKey.tan: That is $\tfrac{12}{35}$, opposite over adjacent, the tangent. Sine divides by the hypotenuse, the 37 m wire.
byKey.cos: That is $\tfrac{35}{37}$, the cosine. The drop is opposite $\theta$, so $\sin\theta = \tfrac{12}{37}$.
byKey.flipped: You divided the hypotenuse by the drop. A sine is never above 1: $\sin\theta = \tfrac{12}{37}$.

explain.text: Seen from the angle $\theta$, the 12 m drop is opposite and the 37 m wire is the hypotenuse. So $\sin\theta = \tfrac{12}{37}$. The ratio belongs to the angle, so it holds for every stretch of the wire.

parts.question: A rider stops 20 m along the wire from the start. Using $\sin\theta = \tfrac{12}{37}$, how far below the start platform is the rider? Give your answer in metres to 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The 20 m of wire is a hypotenuse with the same angle. So the drop is $20 \times \tfrac{12}{37} \approx 6.49$ m.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The 20 m of wire is a hypotenuse, and the drop is opposite the angle.

byKey.cos: That is $20 \times \tfrac{35}{37}$, the distance across. The drop is opposite $\theta$, so use the sine.
byKey.tan: You used $\tfrac{12}{35}$, the tangent. The 20 m runs along the wire, the hypotenuse, so use $\sin\theta = \tfrac{12}{37}$.
byKey.height: That is the rider’s height above the ground, $14 - 6.49$. The question asks how far below the start platform: 6.49 m.

explain.text: The stretch of wire to the rider makes a smaller right-angled triangle with the same angle $\theta$. Its opposite side is the drop, so the drop is $20\sin\theta = 20 \times \tfrac{12}{37} \approx 6.49$ m. Check: 20 m is just over half the wire, and 6.49 m is just over half of 12 m.

parts.question: The rider has dropped 6.49 m along 20 m of wire. How far is the rider from the start platform, measured along the level ground? Give your answer in metres to 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $\sqrt{20^2 - 6.49^2} = \sqrt{357.88} \approx 18.92$ m. The ratio route agrees: $20 \times \tfrac{35}{37} \approx 18.92$ m.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The 20 m of wire is the hypotenuse and the drop is one short side.

byKey.subtracted: You took 6.49 from 20. Lengths do not subtract like that: subtract their squares, then take the root.
byKey.added: You added the squares. The 20 m of wire is the hypotenuse, so subtract: $20^2 - 6.49^2$.

explain.text: The 20 m of wire is the hypotenuse and the drop of 6.49 m is one short side. Subtract squares: $20^2 - 6.49^2 = 357.88$, and $\sqrt{357.88} \approx 18.92$ m. That is a little over half the 35 m gap, as it should be.

items.prose: A floor tile is a regular hexagon ABCDEF with sides of 10 cm. Lines from its centre O to the six corners cut it into six equilateral triangles, each with sides of 10 cm.

parts.question: Cut one of the equilateral triangles down the middle. What is the height of the triangle, exactly, in centimetres?

feedback.correct: Half the triangle has hypotenuse 10 and base 5, so the height is $\sqrt{100 - 25} = \sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}$ cm.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The half-triangle has hypotenuse 10 and base 5. Use Pythagoras and keep the root.

byKey.added: You added the squares. The side of 10 cm is the hypotenuse of the half-triangle, so subtract: $10^2 - 5^2 = 75$.
byKey.whole-side: That uses a hypotenuse of 20. The half-triangle has hypotenuse 10 and base 5, so the height is $\sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}$.
byKey.half-square: That is the half-square’s pattern. The half of an equilateral triangle has sides 5, $5\sqrt{3}$ and 10.

explain.text: Cutting an equilateral triangle down the middle gives a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 10 and base 5. Pythagoras gives height$^2 = 10^2 - 5^2 = 75$. So the height is $\sqrt{75} = \sqrt{25 \times 3} = 5\sqrt{3}$ cm.

parts.question: The line OB cuts the diagonal AC in half, at right angles. Each half of AC is a height of an equilateral triangle, $5\sqrt{3}$ cm. How long is AC, exactly, in centimetres?

feedback.generic: Not quite. AC is made of two halves, each $5\sqrt{3}$ cm.

byKey.half: That is one half of AC. The line OB cuts AC into two halves, so double it.
byKey.side: That is a side of the tile. AC skips the corner B, so it is longer: $2 \times 5\sqrt{3}$.
byKey.long: That is AD, the long diagonal through O. AC is made of two heights, $2 \times 5\sqrt{3}$.

explain.text: A and C are each 10 cm from both O and B. That makes OB cut AC into equal halves at right angles. Each half is a height of an equilateral triangle, $5\sqrt{3}$, so $AC = 10\sqrt{3}$ cm.

parts.question: The long diagonal AD runs through O, so AD = 20 cm, and CD is a side, 10 cm. Using $AC = 10\sqrt{3}$, what is $AC^2 + CD^2$? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each length before adding.

byKey.root-as-three: You squared $10\sqrt{3}$ as $10 \times 3 = 30$. Square both factors: $10^2 \times (\sqrt{3})^2 = 100 \times 3 = 300$.
byKey.root-left: You squared $10\sqrt{3}$ as $100\sqrt{3}$. The square of $\sqrt{3}$ is 3, so $(10\sqrt{3})^2 = 300$.
byKey.cd-unsquared: You added CD itself, 10. Square it as well: $300 + 100 = 400$.

explain.text: Square each factor: $(10\sqrt{3})^2 = 10^2 \times (\sqrt{3})^2 = 100 \times 3 = 300$. Adding $CD^2 = 100$ gives 400. That is $AD^2 = 20^2$, so triangle ACD has a right angle at C.

parts.question: Part 3 gave $AC^2 + CD^2 = 400 = AD^2$, so triangle ACD has a right angle at C. What is the angle CAD, in degrees? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: $\sin CAD = \tfrac{CD}{AD} = \tfrac{10}{20} = \tfrac{1}{2}$, and $\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac{1}{2}$, so the angle is $30^\circ$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Name the sides from A: CD is opposite and AD is the hypotenuse.

byKey.angle-d: 60° is the angle at D, where CD is adjacent. At A, CD is opposite, so $\sin CAD = \tfrac{10}{20}$ and the angle is 30°.
byKey.tan: You used $\tan = \tfrac{10}{20}$, but AD is the hypotenuse, not the adjacent side. Use $\sin CAD = \tfrac{10}{20}$.
byKey.radians: That is the angle in radians, from a calculator in radian mode. Set it to degrees: the angle is 30°.

explain.text: From A, the side CD is opposite and AD is the hypotenuse. So $\sin CAD = \tfrac{1}{2}$, the exact value of $\sin 30^\circ$ from the half-equilateral triangle. The cosine agrees: $\tfrac{AC}{AD} = \tfrac{10\sqrt{3}}{20} = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \cos 30^\circ$.

items.prose: A surveyor stands at a point P on the shore of a lake. She measures to two marker posts, A and B, on the far side. P is 60 m from A and 45 m from B, and the angle APB is $55^\circ$.

parts.question: No angle of triangle APB is known to be a right angle. Which rule finds the distance AB?

options.text: The cosine rule, with the angle between the two sides
The sine rule, since an angle is known
options.why: The sine rule needs a known side together with the angle facing it. The $55^\circ$ angle faces AB, which is the unknown.

options.text: Pythagoras’ theorem on the sides 60 and 45
options.why: Pythagoras needs a right angle. The angle at P is $55^\circ$, not $90^\circ$.
Tangent links sides of a right-angled triangle only, and triangle APB has no right angle.

feedback.correct: Two sides and the angle between them is the cosine rule’s case.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at where the $55^\circ$ angle sits compared with the two known sides.

explain.text: The angle of $55^\circ$ sits between the two known sides, 60 and 45. The cosine rule uses exactly that: $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$. The sine rule would need a known side with the angle facing it.

parts.question: Use the cosine rule with $\cos 55^\circ \approx 0.5736$. How far apart are the posts A and B? Give your answer in metres to 2 decimal places.

widget.accept: 50.27 (50.28, from the unrounded cosine, is also accepted)

feedback.generic: Not quite. Write $AB^2 = 60^2 + 45^2 - 2 \times 60 \times 45 \cos 55^\circ$, then take the root.

byKey.no-root: That is $AB^2$. Take the square root: about 50.27 m.
byKey.plus: You added $2ab\cos C$. The rule subtracts it: $5625 - 3097.44$.
byKey.pythagoras: 75 m is $\sqrt{60^2 + 45^2}$, which needs a right angle at P. Take away $2 \times 60 \times 45 \times \cos 55^\circ$ as well.

explain.text: $60^2 + 45^2 = 5625$, and $2 \times 60 \times 45 \times 0.5736 = 3097.44$. So $AB^2 = 5625 - 3097.44 = 2527.56$ and $AB \approx 50.27$ m. That is less than 75 m because the angle at P is less than a right angle.

parts.question: Using AB ≈ 50.27 m and $\sin 55^\circ \approx 0.8192$, find the angle PAB with the sine rule. Give your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. In the sine rule, pair each side with the angle facing it.

byKey.wrong-side: That angle faces the 60 m side, so it is the angle at B. At A the facing side is PB = 45 m: $\sin A = \tfrac{45 \times 0.8192}{50.27}$.
byKey.ratio: That is $\sin A$. Use the inverse sine to turn it into an angle.
byKey.radians: That is the angle in radians, from a calculator in radian mode. Set it to degrees: about $47.2^\circ$.

explain.text: PB = 45 m faces the angle at A, and AB faces the $55^\circ$ at P. So $\tfrac{\sin A}{45} = \tfrac{0.8192}{50.27}$, which gives $\sin A \approx 0.7333$. The inverse sine gives $A \approx 47.2^\circ$.

parts.question: The shortest path from P to the line through the posts meets that line at a right angle. Using angle PAB ≈ 47.2° and PA = 60 m, how long is that path? Give your answer in metres to 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: PA is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle at A, so the path is $60\sin 47.2^\circ \approx 44.0$ m.
feedback.generic: Not quite. In the right-angled triangle at A, PA is the hypotenuse and the path is opposite the angle at A.

byKey.cos: That is $60\cos 47.2^\circ$, the distance along the line from A. The path from P is opposite the angle at A, so use the sine.
byKey.used-45: You paired 45 m with the angle at A. PA = 60 m is the hypotenuse of the triangle at A: $60\sin 47.2^\circ$.
byKey.tan: You used the tangent. PA = 60 m is the hypotenuse here, so the path is $60\sin 47.2^\circ$.

explain.text: The path meets AB at a right angle, so PA = 60 m is a hypotenuse. The path is opposite the $47.2^\circ$ at A, so it is $60\sin 47.2^\circ \approx 44.0$ m. The angle at B, $180^\circ - 55^\circ - 47.2^\circ = 77.8^\circ$, gives the same: $45\sin 77.8^\circ \approx 44.0$ m.

items.prose: A desk lamp has a lower arm OA of 40 cm, hinged at O on the desk. The arm is raised at $60^\circ$ to the desk. An upper arm AB of 30 cm is fixed at right angles to OA. It leans forward and down to the bulb at B.

parts.question: How high above the desk is the elbow A? Give the exact value in centimetres, without a calculator.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The arm is a hypotenuse, and the height is opposite the $60^\circ$ angle.

byKey.sin-30: That is $40 \times \tfrac{1}{2}$, the value of $\sin 30^\circ$. The height is opposite the $60^\circ$ angle: $40\sin 60^\circ$.
byKey.no-half: You used $\sin 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}$. It is $\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, from the half-equilateral triangle with sides 1, $\sqrt{3}$ and 2.
byKey.half-square: That uses $\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, the value at $45^\circ$. At $60^\circ$ the sine is $\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

explain.text: The arm OA is a hypotenuse, with the height opposite the $60^\circ$. From the half-equilateral triangle, $\sin 60^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. So the height is $40 \times \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 20\sqrt{3}$ cm.

parts.question: The arms meet at a right angle at A. How far is the bulb B from the hinge O, in a straight line? Give a whole number of centimetres.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Triangle OAB has its right angle at A.

byKey.added: You added the arms. OB is the hypotenuse of triangle OAB: $\sqrt{40^2 + 30^2}$.
byKey.subtracted: You subtracted the squares. The right angle is at A, so OB faces it and is the hypotenuse: add the squares.

explain.text: Triangle OAB has its right angle at A, so OB is its hypotenuse. $40^2 + 30^2 = 1600 + 900 = 2500$. So $OB = 50$ cm, the 3, 4, 5 triangle scaled by 10.

parts.question: Triangle OAB has OA = 40 cm, AB = 30 cm and a right angle at A. Find the angle AOB between the lower arm and the line OB. Give your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. From O, the upper arm is opposite and the lower arm is adjacent.

byKey.flipped: That is $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{40}{30}$, the angle at B. From O, AB is opposite and OA is adjacent: $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{30}{40}$.
byKey.sine: You used $\sin^{-1}\tfrac{30}{40}$, but 40 cm is not the hypotenuse. Use $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{30}{40}$, or $\sin^{-1}\tfrac{30}{50}$.
byKey.radians: That is the angle in radians, from a calculator in radian mode. Set it to degrees: about $36.9^\circ$.

explain.text: From O, the side AB = 30 is opposite and OA = 40 is adjacent. So $\tan AOB = 0.75$ and $AOB = \tan^{-1} 0.75 \approx 36.9^\circ$. With OB = 50 from part 2, $\sin^{-1}\tfrac{30}{50}$ gives the same angle.

parts.question: The lower arm is $60^\circ$ above the desk, and OB lies $36.9^\circ$ below the lower arm. Using OB = 50 cm, how high above the desk is the bulb? Give your answer in centimetres to 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: OB is $60^\circ - 36.9^\circ = 23.1^\circ$ above the desk, so the bulb is $50\sin 23.1^\circ \approx 19.6$ cm up.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the angle between OB and the desk first.

byKey.angle-aob: You used $36.9^\circ$ as the angle with the desk. That angle is measured from the arm: OB is $60^\circ - 36.9^\circ = 23.1^\circ$ above the desk.
byKey.sixty: That uses $60^\circ$, the lower arm’s angle. OB is lower: $60^\circ - 36.9^\circ = 23.1^\circ$.
byKey.cos: That is $50\cos 23.1^\circ$, the distance across the desk. The height is opposite the angle, so use the sine.
byKey.added: You added the angles. OB lies below the lower arm, so take $36.9^\circ$ away from $60^\circ$.

explain.text: OB lies below the lower arm, so its angle with the desk is $60^\circ - 36.9^\circ = 23.1^\circ$. OB is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle on the desk, with the height opposite that angle. So the height is $50\sin 23.1^\circ \approx 19.6$ cm.

parts.question: Now check part 4 exactly. The upper arm points $30^\circ$ below the level, since it is at right angles to the lower arm. Starting from the elbow height $20\sqrt{3}$ cm, write the exact height of the bulb above the desk, in centimetres.

feedback.correct: The bulb is $30\sin 30^\circ = 15$ cm below the elbow, so its height is $20\sqrt{3} - 15 \approx 19.64$ cm, which matches part 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find how far the upper arm drops, then take it from the elbow height.

byKey.above: The upper arm leans down, so the bulb is 15 cm below the elbow: $20\sqrt{3} - 15$.
byKey.cos-30: You took away $30\cos 30^\circ = 15\sqrt{3}$. The drop is opposite the $30^\circ$, so it is $30\sin 30^\circ = 15$.
byKey.whole-arm: You took away the whole arm. The arm slopes at $30^\circ$, so it drops only $30\sin 30^\circ = 15$ cm.

explain.text: AB is the hypotenuse of a small right-angled triangle hanging from A, with the drop opposite the $30^\circ$. Since $\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac{1}{2}$, the drop is $30 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 15$ cm. So the bulb is $20\sqrt{3} - 15 \approx 34.64 - 15 = 19.64$ cm above the desk.
